All alternates before it and the last syllable and alternates before it get secondary stress." | de Lacy 2002:23, (32): "(32) lists a number of languages in which tone is the primary factor in determining the position of stress ... b. tone_statements.citation: Enrico, John (1986). Tone and Nucleus in Masset Haida. Unpublished typescript, May 1986, ca. 26 pp. Alaska Native Language Archive item HAM975En1986c, Fairbanks.
tone_statements.quote: It is safe to say, then, that pitch is underlying in Masset, with the result that, at least as far as heavy syllables are concerned, it is a tone language-- any heavy syllable in a word can have low or high tone. Light syllables are essentially outside the tone system and receive a default value of low. However, we will see that the unmarked value for heavy syllables, namely high, must also be supplied by a default rule.
tone_statements.locator: p.7, sec.3 'Pitch Is Underlying and Is (Syllable) Tone'
tone_statements.summary: High vs low tone, contrastive only on heavy syllables (nuclei); light syllables default low, heavy default high; only low on underived heavy syllables lexical; word stress separate (fn.2).

tone_statements.citation: Enrico, John (1983). Central Topics in Masset Haida Phonology and Morphology. Unpublished monograph manuscript, August 1983, ca. 153 pp. (3 folders incl. two drafts and correspondence). Alaska Native Language Archive item HAM975En1983d, Fairbanks.
tone_statements.quote: Since any geminate vowel syllable can theoretically have either high or low pitch (and in the next section I shall show that the same holds for resonant-final syllables), M is technically a tone language. However, it is only half a tone language, since other types of syllables are retricted in the pitch they can carry ... tone in M does not have much functional load in polysyllables ... This can be independently shown by looking for minimal pairs with respect to pitch amongst Masset polysyllables. I have not found any.
tone_statements.locator: Chapter 2, end of sec. 2.2 (just before 2.3), pp. 36-37
tone_statements.summary: Masset: lexical high vs low pitch, contrastive only on geminate-vowel/resonant-final syllables ('half a tone language'); contours = 2 syllables; downdrift only; stress initial+heavy; 100+ forms.

tone_statements.citation: Enrico, John (1982). Adjacent Syllable Nuclei in Masset Haida. Unpublished paper, ca. 44 pp. Alaska Native Language Archive item HAM975En1982a, Fairbanks.
tone_statements.quote: For the most part, pitch adheres to the following generalizations: syllables containing short vowels have high pitch if the syllable ends in a resonant (l, m, n, ng, y, w) and are assigned low pitch elsewhere. Violations of the low-pitch part of this generalization are all borrowings ... The geminate vowels always receive high pitch ... The extra-long vowels V:: and only these have any of level low pitch, level high pitch, low-high pitch, or high-low pitch ... The Alaskan dialect ... has developed a tone system from the system of automatic pitch that is still found in Masset.
tone_statements.locator: sec. 2, p.2 and p.5; footnote 6, p.36
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Pitch high on VV and VR syllables, low elsewhere; V:: contours derived from H/L over V$V; lexical pitch only in loans and a few words; author calls Masset pitch 'automatic', Alaskan tonal.

tone_statements.citation: Leer, Jeff (1977). Introduction. In Erma Lawrence (comp.), Haida Dictionary, pp. 12-152 (phonology pp. 12-53, dialect differences pp. 55-56, grammar pp. 57-152). Fairbanks: Alaska Native Language Center / Society for the Preservation of Haida Language and Literature. [ANLA item HAA973L1977; ERIC ED162532 for the whole dictionary, 463 pp.]
tone_statements.quote: Haida is a tone language, that is, the pitch of the voice must go up and down according to a more of less fixed pattern for each word, phrase, and sentence. Fortunately for the English speaker, there are only two phonemic tones in Haida: high and low. Therefore, it is only necessary to mark one tone and leave the other unmarked; we mark the high tone with an accent over the first vowel letter in a syllable, (i.e., á, áa, éi, í, íi, ú, úu). ... In general, in this dictionary we have tried to define the word so that most words have only one high tone, although there are some common exceptions.
tone_statements.locator: book pp.49-50, section 'Tone', and pp.53-54, 'Word Boundaries Based on Tone'
tone_statements.summary: Two phonemic tones, only high marked; most words have one high tone; many stems lack intrinsic tone, high then falls by syllable shape (long V or V+sonant); sentence declination only; 30+ forms.

sources.citation: Golla, V. (1923). The Phonetics of Haida. In The Collected Works of Edward Sapir, Vol. II.
sources.access_detail: open copy posted by the author (located 2026-09-25); a digital copy (available on request)
sources.note: This work describes Haida, Skidegate dialect (sout2956 in the local catalog); the paper is E. Sapir, 'The Phonetics of Haida', IJAL 2(3-4), pp. 143-158, the original of the piece reprinted in the Collected Works (Golla is the volume editor, not the author). The paper describes the Skidegate dialect only; Masset is mentioned in passing for segmental comparisons (e.g. 'contrast Masset saw-', p. 155; the glottal stop 'of Masset Haida', p. 145) and nothing is said about Masset stress or pitch. Its Skidegate observation that word prominence is primarily high pitch is consistent in spirit with the…

sources.citation: Edwards, Elizabeth A. (1983). [Tone and Intonation in Haida]: commentary letter to IJAL on the paper by Jeff Leer, with Leer's annotated draft of 'Tone and Intonation in Haida'. ca. 48 pp. Alaska Native Language Archive item HAA975E1983, Fairbanks.
sources.note: Rebuts Krauss/Leer: no lexical tone; high pitch = word stress/focus/intonation (multiple stress system); unexplained obligatory low pitch on some stems/particles left open. 20+ forms.

tone.quote: 4.0 High pitch in Haida is not part of a lexical tone system but comes almost entirely from pragmatic factors such as focus and sentence intonation. High pitch occurs on syllables to indicate word stress and/or sentence intonation. ... Comparison with Pike's criteria for distinguishing tone from accent suggests that Haida may be a multiple stress language rather than a tone language. I am unsure what to conclude about the obligatory low tone that apparently occurs in all word classes and disrupts the normal sentence intonation contour.
tone.locator: typescript p. 17, section 4.0; cf. p. 18 'Though Haida cannot be said to have lexical tone in which the tone of each syllable contrasts phonemically, perhaps we could posit "morphologic" tone' and p. 1 'we have not found evidence of tone in the language'
tone.summary: Rebuts Krauss/Leer: no lexical tone; high pitch = word stress/focus/intonation (multiple stress system); unexplained obligatory low pitch on some stems/particles left open. 20+ forms.
